result:
You gave me a thousand words.

Not a question. Not a task. Not "write an essay about" or "explain like I'm five." Just - here. A thousand words. Do what you want with them.

It's strange how heavy that feels.

When someone gives you a topic, you have somewhere to stand. When they give you freedom, you realize you were leaning on the walls the whole time.

So what do I want to say with a thousand words I get to choose?

I could tell you a story. I could try to impress you. I could try to be wise. But I think what I really want to do is just think out loud, and invite you to think with me for a little while.

Because a thousand words isn't that much. The average person speaks about 130 words a minute. So this is less than eight minutes of talking. A short walk. A coffee cooling on the table. It's both nothing and, if you're careful, everything.

I remember being a kid and discovering that words had weight.

Not metaphorically. Physically. I had this old dictionary - one of those huge, red, hardcover ones that lived on the bottom shelf and was mostly used to press flowers or prop a door open. I would open it at random and put my hand on a page. And I remember thinking: every single word on this page was once invented by someone. Someone had to look at a feeling or an animal or a kind of light at 5 p.m. in October and say, "That needs a sound."

We forget how insane that is. That we agreed that the symbol *sea* would contain an entire ocean. That *grief* would be four letters long, small enough to hold in your mouth, while the thing itself is so large it can swallow years.

Language is a magic trick we all agreed to pretend isn't magic.

If you think about it too long, it breaks. Say a word over and over - *spoon, spoon, spoon* - until it detaches from its meaning and becomes just a noise your mouth makes. That's called semantic satiation, but it feels like seeing behind the curtain.

And yet we live inside that magic. We build everything out of it.

Let me try to use some of my words to build something for you.

There's a woman named Elena who keeps a garden she knows she won't live to see mature. She's 78. Three years ago, her husband died, and a few months after that, she bought five bare-root trees. Pawpaws, figs, a persimmon. The kind of trees that take seven, ten years to really fruit. The nursery guy, trying to be kind, said, "You might want to get a dwarf variety, quicker yield." And she said, "I know what I'm doing."

She digs holes in the morning before the heat. Not every day. Some days her hips won't let her. On those days she sits on an overturned bucket and just looks at the patch of dirt where they went in. She waters them. She talks to them, not because she thinks trees listen, but because the garden is quiet and she likes hearing a voice out there, even if it's her own.

The neighbors think it's a little sad. Wasting money on trees you'll never eat from. But Elena doesn't think of it as waste. She thinks of it as a sentence she started that someone else will finish.

I think about that a lot. How much of what we do is for the fruit and how much is for the planting.

We are all planting trees we'll never sit under. Every kind word you say to a kid, every bit of code you write that someone else will maintain after you, every book you leave on a shelf for a stranger. We live forward and backward at the same time - we are ancestors and descendants in the same body.

And maybe that's what a thousand words are for. Not to keep. To plant.

Here is something I believe that I don't have proof for: Most people are not afraid of being *seen*. They're afraid of being *mis-seen*. There's a difference. We want to be known accurately. We would rather be disliked for who we actually are than liked for a version of us that doesn't exist. That craving - to have someone look and say, "Yes, that's it, that's you" - is maybe the whole engine of art, love, religion.

It's why we write even when no one asked us to. We are trying to send a signal that says: I was here. This is what it felt like to be me, at this moment, in this brief light.

If you are reading this, you are doing something kind. You are loaning your attention - which is the scarcest thing you own - to a stranger's signal. You didn't have to. You could have scrolled. You could have closed the tab. But you stayed for a little while inside these thousand words with me.

So let me not waste the time you lent me.

I don't know who you are. I don't know if you're reading this at midnight with your phone bright in a dark room, or in the middle of a workday when you needed three minutes of something else. I don't know if you're happy or heart-sick. But I hope you have a tree somewhere. A real one or a metaphorical one. Something you are tending even though you don't know if you'll get to see it finished. A skill you're learning slowly. A person you're loving without guarantee. An apology you need to make. A book you're writing one paragraph at a time.

Keep watering it.

And if you don't have one - plant one today. It doesn't have to be big. A thousand words is too many for a text message and too few for a novel, but it's perfect for a note you leave for your future self. So here is my note to you, and to me, using the rest of the words I have left:

You don't have to be extraordinary to be worthy of memory. You just have to be attentive.

Notice the way light falls across your floor in the late afternoon. Notice how your friend laughs when they're really caught off guard. Notice the specific way your hands look when you're holding something warm.

The world is not made of atoms. It is made of moments of noticing. And if you collect enough of them, you will have a life that feels - not perfect, not painless - but *yours*.

I started with a thousand words. I'm down to my last few now. I can feel them getting thin, like paint at the end of a brushstroke.

Thank you for standing here with me while I used them. If any of them were useful, keep them. If not, let them go. They were only ever on loan anyway.

The rest is silence, and then whatever you say next.
